title: Speech Writing — salutation, hooks, persuasive devices
notes: **What it is:** writing meant to be SPOKEN — short sentences, rhythm, direct address. The examiner checks 'speakability'.

**Structure:** Salutation in order of seniority ('Respected Chairperson, judges, teachers, and my dear friends —') → Self-intro (if required) → Hook (question/fact/quotation) → 2–3 clear points ('First… Second… Finally…') → Persuasive devices (triads, repetition, rhetorical questions) → Strong closing appeal + 'Thank you.'
**Grammar for the ear:** imperatives command action ('Let us pledge…'); rhetorical questions make the audience answer mentally; triads create rhythm.
**Test:** read your draft aloud — where you gasp, rewrite. Repeat your core phrase 2–3 times.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

**Speech blueprint (classified)**

| Section | Job | Device |
|---|---|---|
| Opening | Hook the room | Question, fact, anecdote |
| Roadmap | Tell them what’s coming | Three-part preview |
| Body | One point per section | Rule of three, repetition |
| Close | Call to action | Callback to opening |

**Spoken-language features**

| Feature | Example | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Direct address | Friends, look around you | Connection |
| Rhetorical question | What would you do? | Thinking aloud |
| Tripling | blood, sweat and tears | Rhythm and force |
| Contrast | Not left, but right | Memorable punch |

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Speech frame: greeting → attention hook (question/quote/statistic) → three points with signposting ('firstly... secondly...') → memorable close (call to action).
Trick 2: Write for the EAR: short sentences, direct address ('my friends'), rhetorical questions — spoken rhythm is the style mark.
Trick 3: Time yourself: a 3-minute speech ≈ 350–400 words — over-length speeches lose the discipline mark.
practiceQuestions: Q. Prepare a 2-minute speech on the importance of voting. (4 marks) — greeting, hook, two arguments, call to action.
Q. How should a speech begin? (1 mark) — with a greeting and an attention-grabbing hook.
